```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

This vignette runs one binary scale from raw data frame to a table you could
paste into a manuscript. It uses the Scientific Reasoning Scale, which the
package ships.

## The data

Eleven binary items answered by 337 respondents in an Italian validation study
(Caliciuri & Lanz, 2024, CC BY 4.0; see `?srs` for the full provenance and
`bm_cite()` for the citation to use).

```{r data}
data(srs)
dim(srs)
srs[1:4, 1:6]
```

Items are already scored 0/1 in the direction the instrument intends. That is
worth checking rather than assuming, which is what the next step is for.

## Screen before you fit

```{r check}
bm_check_data(srs)
```

`bm_check_data()` is not a formality. It reports the things that quietly change
an answer: item types, how many respondents survive complete-scale filtering,
constant items, and items whose relationship with the rest of the scale runs
backwards.

**On reverse keying.** The screen *reports* candidates; it does not fix them.
That is deliberate. Published instruments very often arrive already scored, and
a package that silently flipped items would corrupt exactly the datasets that
were prepared most carefully. When you do need to recode, say so explicitly:

```{r score-map, eval = FALSE}
# Only if your own items need it -- the SRS does not.
sm <- bm_score_map(srs, reverse = c("SRS3", "SRS7"))
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, score_map = sm, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
```

## The coefficient, without an interval

`mokken_h()` computes the coefficient and nothing else. It is deterministic,
instant, and a good first look.

```{r deterministic}
emp <- mokken_h(srs, warn = FALSE)
emp
```

The object carries the three levels of the analysis:

```{r structure}
bm_scale_h(emp)
head(bm_item_h(emp), 3)
head(bm_pair_h(emp), 3)
```

## The interval

```{r fit}
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
bm_interval(fit)
```

### Choosing the number of draws

`draws` controls Monte Carlo noise in the endpoints, not the width of the
interval. The question is how many are enough for the endpoints to stop moving:

```{r fig-stability, fig.alt = "Interval endpoints plotted against the number of Bayesian-bootstrap draws, showing both endpoints flattening as the draw count grows."}
bm_plot_mc_stability(fit)
```

`bm_mc_diagnostics()` puts a number on the same thing:

```{r mc}
bm_mc_diagnostics(fit)
```

Read the endpoint Monte Carlo standard errors against the precision you intend
to report. If you report three decimals, you want simulation noise well below
the third.

### What the correction did

```{r fig-draws, fig.alt = "Bootstrap distribution of the scalability coefficient with the uncorrected and corrected interval endpoints drawn beneath it, showing the corrected endpoints slightly further apart."}
bm_plot_draws(fit)
```

```{r width}
iv <- bm_interval(fit)
c(raw_width = iv$raw_upper - iv$raw_lower,
  calibrated_width = iv$upper - iv$lower,
  multiplier = iv$width_multiplier)
```

The multiplier here is `r fmt_h(iv$width_multiplier, 4)`, a change of
`r fmt_width_change(iv)`. It follows $1 + 0.25/\sqrt{n}$, so it shrinks as the
sample grows: the uncorrected interval was found to be slightly too narrow, and
the shortfall it repairs is itself a small-sample effect.
`vignette("m2-bayesian-bootstrap-calibration")` derives it.

The midpoint is untouched. The correction only ever changes length.

## Reproducing the published interval

The article reports this scale at 50,000 draws. That fit is cached, so this
vignette can show it without a long bootstrap:

```{r published}
published <- bm_cached("srs_50000")
bm_interval(published)
```

```{r published-note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("<p><em>", bm_cached_note("srs_50000"), "</em></p>", sep = "")
```

One honest caveat, stated in that note and worth repeating: the article's own
draws came from the research harness rather than from `bb_mokken_h()`, so the
endpoints agree to Monte Carlo error, not exactly. The opt-in published-number
gate checks this when the runner is invoked as
`Rscript inst/scripts/run-all-gates.R --published`. The ordinary runner does
not read external research sources; its mandatory G-10 instead rebuilds and
deep-diffs the shipped cache from an isolated current-source installation.

Note also how little the interval moved between 2,000 and 50,000 draws:

```{r compare-draws}
rbind(`2,000 draws`  = c(lower = iv$lower, upper = iv$upper),
      `50,000 draws` = c(lower = bm_interval(published)$lower,
                         upper = bm_interval(published)$upper))
```

That is the point of the stability plot above. Draws buy precision in the
*answer about* the interval, not a different interval.

## Diagnostics

```{r diagnostics}
bm_diagnostics(fit)
```

The denominator section deserves attention. $H$ is a ratio, and a pair whose
maximum attainable covariance is near zero contributes a near-zero denominator.
Such pairs are reported rather than dropped, because dropping them silently
would change the estimand without saying so.

```{r regularity}
head(bm_regularity(fit), 4)
```

## Reporting

```{r report}
bm_report(fit, what = "scale", format = "markdown")
```

```{r report-items}
head(bm_report(fit, what = "item", format = "data.frame", digits = 3)$table, 4)
```

And to place the estimate against the conventional landmarks:

```{r benchmark}
bm_benchmark(fit)
```

`bm_benchmark()` reports a point relation and nothing more. Its output contains
no verdict about the scale, because the landmarks are descriptive conventions
rather than decision rules, and because the software is not in a position to
know what your instrument is for.

## Common errors

**Items stored as text or factors.** A column of `"0"`/`"1"` is not numeric.
Convert before fitting; `bm_check_data()` names the offending columns.

**Missing-value codes left in the data.** Values like `-9` or `99` are
ordinary numbers to R. Declare them:

```{r missing, eval = FALSE}
mc <- bm_missing_codes(items = names(srs), codes = c(-9, 99))
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, missing_codes = mc, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
```

**A constant item.** An item everyone answered the same way has zero variance
and cannot contribute to a covariance ratio. The screen flags it; remove it and
refit, remembering that you have then declared a different scale.

**Reverse-keyed items.** Covered above. Report, inspect, then recode
deliberately.

**Refitting after dropping an item.** Legitimate, but it defines a new
analysis. The interval from the eleven-item scale says nothing about the
ten-item one, and `bm_compare()` will refuse to line the two up unless you pass
`allow_different = TRUE` to say you meant it.
